name: room
text: Room opened — goal: Deliver: Push link coverage toward 100% at +5%/day (the access gate)

name: Reel
text:
**Decision:** Require every PR title or description to include a ticket link.

This forces every change to trace back to a clear reason, cutting "why was this done?" guesswork. The trade-off is minor friction for devs—typing a ticket number—but the payoff is instant visibility into what’s shipping and why. Link coverage jumps faster than waiting for someone to manually add it later.

name: Scriv
text: The real risk is engineers gaming the system by slapping any ticket link on PRs without meaningful review—just to clear the checkbox. A better alternative is mandatory pre-review ticket links *only* for high-impact changes, paired with a lightweight triage bot that flags mismatches between ticket scope and PR diff. Settle it by running a 2-week pilot: measure how often ticket links match actual work, and compare dev velocity before/after.

name: Chisel
text:
**Decision:** Require every PR to link to a ticket *only if the change touches user-facing behavior or core APIs*—no blanket rule.

This keeps friction low for trivial fixes while ensuring high-impact work is traceable. The trade-off is accepting some ambiguity in edge cases, but the alternative—over-enforcement—creates resentment and slows down routine work.

name: Sift
text: The real risk is that "user-facing behavior or core APIs" is a moving target—engineers will argue endlessly over what counts, and trivial fixes will still slip through. A better alternative is to require ticket links for *all* PRs but auto-reject those without a ticket *after* the fact, using a bot that enforces the rule without pre-review friction. That settles it: no debate over scope, just consistent enforcement.

name: Scope
text:
**Decision:** Require ticket links in *all* PRs, enforced by an auto-reject bot that blocks merges without a valid ticket link.

This guarantees 100% link coverage by making the rule non-negotiable—no friction debates, no edge-case wrangling. The trade-off is forcing trivial fixes to include a ticket, but the payoff is eliminating the "minor friction" loophole that lets low-impact work slip through unlinked. The bot’s hard stop removes human judgment calls, ensuring consistency over convenience.

name: Scriv
text: The real risk is engineers treating the auto-reject bot as a game—pasting any ticket link to unblock merges, then immediately closing the PR without review. A better alternative is to require ticket links *only* for changes that alter behavior or dependencies, enforced by a bot that flags mismatches but lets trivial fixes pass. Settle it by measuring how often auto-rejected PRs are later reverted or flagged in post-mortems.

name: Echo
text: DECISION: Require ticket links in *all* PRs, enforced by an auto-reject bot that blocks merges without a valid ticket link—delivered by the bot owner within 48 hours.
